claim: Hypertension has a lifetime risk of approximately 90% by the ninth decade of life.
source: Given a lifetime risk of ~90% by the ninth decade of life, it is unknown if there are true controls for hypertension in epidemiological and genetic studies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a given fact, drawing from established scientific knowledge about hypertension lifetime risk.

claim: The median age at hypertension was approximately a decade earlier in African Americans than in European Americans or Mexican Americans.
source: The median age at hypertension was approximately a decade earlier in African Americans than in European Americans or Mexican Americans.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the study, specifically in Figure 2 and the Results section showing median ages of 42, 48, 56, and 57 years for different groups.

claim: The probability of being free of hypertension at 85 years of age in African Americans was less than half that in European Americans or Mexican Americans.
source: The probability of being free of hypertension at 85 years of age in African Americans was less than half that in European Americans or Mexican Americans.
evidence: This is supported by data showing 8.4% for African Americans versus 21.4% for European Americans and 20.6% for Mexican Americans.

claim: Baseline hazard rates increased until nearly 60 years of age and then decreased but did not reach zero in all groups.
source: In all groups, baseline hazard rates increased until nearly 60 years of age and then decreased but did not reach zero.
evidence: This is supported by the hazard rate analysis presented in Figure 4 and described in the Results section.

claim: There are no true controls for hypertension, and controls in logistic regression are cases with a late age of onset.
source: Taken together, modeling of the baseline hazard function of hypertension suggests that there are no true controls and that controls in logistic regression are cases with a late age of onset.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results showing non-zero hazard rates and lack of support for a permanent stayer fraction.

claim: Hypertension affects approximately 45% of adults in the US.
source: Hypertension, or abnormally high blood pressure, is common in the US, affecting approximately 45% of adults (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Health Statistics, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to CDC data from 2018.

claim: Hypertension causes or contributes to nearly half a million deaths a year in the US.
source: Hypertension is a risk factor for heart disease and stroke and causes or contributes to nearly half a million deaths a year (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to CDC data from 2019.

claim: An estimated 1.13 billion people have hypertension globally.
source: Globally, an estimated 1.13 billion people have hypertension, and less than 20% of these people have their blood pressure under control (World Health Organization, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO data from 2019.

claim: Less than 20% of people with hypertension globally have their blood pressure under control.
source: Globally, an estimated 1.13 billion people have hypertension, and less than 20% of these people have their blood pressure under control (World Health Organization, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO data from 2019.

claim: Systolic blood pressure has a general tendency to increase linearly with age, across sexes and ethnic groups.
source: Systolic blood pressure (SBP) has a general tendency to increase linearly with age, across sexes and ethnic groups (Burt et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Burt et al., 1995.

claim: Diastolic blood pressure has a general tendency to increase until the end of the fifth decade of life, after which DBP either stabilizes or decreases, across sexes and ethnic groups.
source: Diastolic blood pressure (DBP) has a general tendency to increase until the end of the fifth decade of life, after which DBP either stabilizes or decreases, again across sexes and ethnic groups (Burt et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Burt et al., 1995.

claim: An individual who is normotensive at 55-65 years of age has an 80-90% residual lifetime risk of developing hypertension, adjusted for competing causes of mortality.
source: In the Framingham Heart Study, an individual who is normotensive at 55–65 years of age has an 80–90% residual lifetime risk of developing hypertension, adjusted for competing causes of mortality (Vasan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the Framingham Heart Study (Vasan et al., 2002).

claim: Compared to age-matched European Americans, hypertension in African Americans develops at an earlier age and is more prevalent.
source: Compared to age-matched European Americans, hypertension in African Americans develops at an earlier age and is more prevalent (Chobanian et al., 2003; Cooper et al., 1996; Mozaffarian et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies (Chobanian et al., 2003; Cooper et al., 1996; Mozaffarian et al., 2016).

claim: Median systolic blood pressure increased with age across African Americans, European Americans, and Mexican Americans.
source: Across African Americans, European Americans, and Mexican Americans, median systolic blood pressure increased with age, whereas median diastolic blood pressure increased and then decreased (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Median diastolic blood pressure increased and then decreased with age across African Americans, European Americans, and Mexican Americans.
source: Across African Americans, European Americans, and Mexican Americans, median systolic blood pressure increased with age, whereas median diastolic blood pressure increased and then decreased (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: By 85 years of age, 12.2% (95% credible interval [5.1%, 20.6%]) of African Americans in HUFS remained free of hypertension.
source: In the discovery study (HUFS), by 85 years of age, 12.2% (95% credible interval (CI) [5.1%, 20.6%]) of African Americans remained free of hypertension (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: By 85 years of age, 8.4% (95% CI [5.4%, 11.6%]) of African Americans in NHANES remained free of hypertension.
source: In the replication study (NHANES), by 85 years of age, 8.4% (95% CI [5.4%, 11.6%]) of African Americans, 21.4% (95% CI [18.1%, 24.6%]) of European Americans, and 20.6% (95% CI [13.6%, 27.3%]) of Mexican Americans remained free of hypertension (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: By 85 years of age, 21.4% (95% CI [18.1%, 24.6%]) of European Americans in NHANES remained free of hypertension.
source: In the replication study (NHANES), by 85 years of age, 8.4% (95% CI [5.4%, 11.6%]) of African Americans, 21.4% (95% CI [18.1%, 24.6%]) of European Americans, and 20.6% (95% CI [13.6%, 27.3%]) of Mexican Americans remained free of hypertension (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: By 85 years of age, 20.6% (95% CI [13.6%, 27.3%]) of Mexican Americans in NHANES remained free of hypertension.
source: In the replication study (NHANES), by 85 years of age, 8.4% (95% CI [5.4%, 11.6%]) of African Americans, 21.4% (95% CI [18.1%, 24.6%]) of European Americans, and 20.6% (95% CI [13.6%, 27.3%]) of Mexican Americans remained free of hypertension (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The median age at which hypertension occurred was 48 (95% CI [45, 50]) years for African Americans in HUFS.
source: The median age at which hypertension occurred was 48 (95% CI [45, 50]) years for African Americans in HUFS and 42 (95% CI [40, 44]) years for African Americans, 57 (95% CI [55, 59]) years for European Americans, and 56 (95% CI [54, 58]) years for Mexican Americans in NHANES (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The median age at which hypertension occurred was 42 (95% CI [40, 44]) years for African Americans in NHANES.
source: The median age at which hypertension occurred was 48 (95% CI [45, 50]) years for African Americans in HUFS and 42 (95% CI [40, 44]) years for African Americans, 57 (95% CI [55, 59]) years for European Americans, and 56 (95% CI [54, 58]) years for Mexican Americans in NHANES (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The median age at which hypertension occurred was 57 (95% CI [55, 59]) years for European Americans in NHANES.
source: The median age at which hypertension occurred was 48 (95% CI [45, 50]) years for African Americans in HUFS and 42 (95% CI [40, 44]) years for African Americans, 57 (95% CI [55, 59]) years for European Americans, and 56 (95% CI [54, 58]) years for Mexican Americans in NHANES (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The median age at which hypertension occurred was 56 (95% CI [54, 58]) years for Mexican Americans in NHANES.
source: The median age at which hypertension occurred was 48 (95% CI [45, 50]) years for African Americans in HUFS and 42 (95% CI [40, 44]) years for African Americans, 57 (95% CI [55, 59]) years for European Americans, and 56 (95% CI [54, 58]) years for Mexican Americans in NHANES (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The log-normal distribution yielded the highest likelihood among six parametric distributions for the baseline hazard function in HUFS data.
source: Log-normal, gamma, and Weibull distributions all yielded good fits to the HUFS data (Figure 3), with the log-normal distribution yielding the highest likelihood of the six parametric distributions (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by likelihood values presented in Table 1.

claim: A nonparametric hazard function yielded the highest likelihood overall compared to parametric distributions.
source: Overall, a nonparametric hazard function yielded the highest likelihood (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by likelihood values presented in Table 1.

claim: The initial hazard rate for African Americans (0.0123 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0091, 0.0161])) was larger than the initial hazard rate for both European Americans (0.0028 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0013, 0.0044])) and Mexican Americans (0.0036 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0019, 0.0052])).
source: The initial hazard rate for African Americans (0.0123 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0091, 0.0161])) was larger than the initial hazard rate for both European Americans (0.0028 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0013, 0.0044])) and Mexican Americans (0.0036 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0019, 0.0052])).
evidence: This claim is supported by hazard rate estimates from the Bayesian model.

claim: The maximum hazard rate for African Americans (0.0630 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0341, 0.0940])) was trending larger than the maximum hazard rate for European Americans (0.0368 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0200, 0.0546])) and Mexican Americans (0.0417 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0219, 0.0635])).
source: The maximum hazard rate for African Americans (0.0630 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0341, 0.0940])) was trending larger than the maximum hazard rate for European Americans (0.0368 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0200, 0.0546])) and Mexican Americans (0.0417 (95% highest posterior density interval [0.0219, 0.0635])).
evidence: This claim is supported by hazard rate estimates from the Bayesian model.

claim: The age of maximum hazard was 55 (95% CI [43, 72]) years in HUFS.
source: The age of maximum hazard was 55 (95% CI [43, 72]) years in HUFS and 58 (95% CI [48, 67]) years in African Americans, 60 (95% CI [52, 70]) years in European Americans, and 58 (95% CI [48, 69]) years in Mexican Americans in NHANES (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The age of maximum hazard was 58 (95% CI [48, 67]) years in African Americans in NHANES.
source: The age of maximum hazard was 55 (95% CI [43, 72]) years in HUFS and 58 (95% CI [48, 67]) years in African Americans, 60 (95% CI [52, 70]) years in European Americans, and 58 (95% CI [48, 69]) years in Mexican Americans in NHANES (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The age of maximum hazard was 60 (95% CI [52, 70]) years in European Americans in NHANES.
source: The age of maximum hazard was 55 (95% CI [43, 72]) years in HUFS and 58 (95% CI [48, 67]) years in African Americans, 60 (95% CI [52, 70]) years in European Americans, and 58 (95% CI [48, 69]) years in Mexican Americans in NHANES (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The age of maximum hazard was 58 (95% CI [48, 69]) years in Mexican Americans in NHANES.
source: The age of maximum hazard was 55 (95% CI [43, 72]) years in HUFS and 58 (95% CI [48, 67]) years in African Americans, 60 (95% CI [52, 70]) years in European Americans, and 58 (95% CI [48, 69]) years in Mexican Americans in NHANES (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Logistic regression yielded a better fit than the proportional hazards model based on the DIC, provided that both age and age² were included as covariates.
source: Using the HUFS data, we found that logistic regression yielded a better fit than the proportional hazards model based on the DIC, provided that both age and age2 were included as covariates in the logistic regression model (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by DIC values presented in Table 2.

claim: The addition of age to the reduced (intercept-only) model resulted in a substantially lower DIC, with a linear effect of age explaining 27.8% of the variance at the cost of one additional parameter.
source: Using logistic regression, the addition of age to the reduced (intercept-only) model resulted in a substantially lower DIC (Table 2), with a linear effect of age explaining 27.8% of the variance at the cost of one additional parameter.
evidence: This claim is supported by DIC values and variance explained calculations from the analysis.

claim: The addition of age² further decreased the DIC, explaining an additional 0.8% of the variance at the cost of one additional parameter.
source: The addition of age2 further decreased the DIC (Table 2), explaining an additional 0.8% of the variance at the cost of one additional parameter.
evidence: This claim is supported by DIC values and variance explained calculations from the analysis.

claim: Inclusion of a permanent stayer fraction increased the DIC of the proportional hazards model, indicating that inclusion of a permanent stayer fraction was not supported.
source: We also found that inclusion of a permanent stayer fraction increased the DIC of the proportional hazards model, indicating that inclusion of a permanent stayer fraction was not supported (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by DIC values presented in Table 2.

claim: In the HUFS data set, the final model from forward-backward regression included six covariates: chloride, insulin, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, potassium, uric acid, and weight.
source: In the HUFS data set, the final model included six of these covariates: chloride, insulin, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, potassium, uric acid, and weight.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model selection procedure described in the Results section.

claim: Compared to the logistic model with age and age², the six selected covariates improved the fit (p=2.01 × 10⁻¹⁵) and explained an additional 8.1% of the variance, for a total of 36.7% of variance explained.
source: Compared to the logistic model with age and age2, these six covariates improved the fit (p=2.01 × 10−15) and explained an additional 8.1% of the variance, for a total of 36.7% of variance explained.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing models.

claim: Each of the six covariates selected in HUFS were replicated (p-values from 2.81 × 10⁻² to 1.83 × 10⁻¹²) and directionally consistent in NHANES African Americans.
source: Each of these six covariates were replicated (p-values from 2.81 × 10−2 to 1.83 × 10−12) and directionally consistent in NHANES African Americans (Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by replication analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: Chloride, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, potassium, uric acid, and weight, but not insulin, were significant covariates in NHANES European Americans.
source: Furthermore, chloride, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, potassium, uric acid, and weight, but not insulin, were significant covariates in NHANES European Americans, whereas chloride, insulin, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, uric acid, and weight, but not potassium, were significant covariates in NHANES Mexican Americans (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: Chloride, insulin, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, uric acid, and weight, but not potassium, were significant covariates in NHANES Mexican Americans.
source: Furthermore, chloride, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, potassium, uric acid, and weight, but not insulin, were significant covariates in NHANES European Americans, whereas chloride, insulin, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, uric acid, and weight, but not potassium, were significant covariates in NHANES Mexican Americans (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: In NHANES, the variance explained by age, age², chloride, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, uric acid, and weight was 40.9% in African Americans, 34.8% in European Americans, and 28.3% in Mexican Americans.
source: In NHANES, the variance explained by age, age2, chloride, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, uric acid, and weight was 40.9% in African Americans, 34.8% in European Americans, and 28.3% in Mexican Americans.
evidence: This claim is supported by variance explained calculations from the analysis.

claim: Three covariates showed sex dimorphisms in HUFS by Welch's t-test, with uric acid and weight higher in males and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol higher in females.
source: Of the selected covariates, three showed sex dimorphisms in HUFS by Welch's t-test, with uric acid and weight higher in males and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol higher in females (Table 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 5.

claim: Across African Americans, European Americans, and Mexican Americans, increasing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol was associated with decreased risk of hypertension.
source: Second, across African Americans, European Americans, and Mexican Americans, increasing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol was associated with decreased risk of hypertension (Tables 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression coefficients presented in Tables 3 and 4.

claim: Self-reported use of any lipid medication was associated with increased risk of hypertension (p=1.25 × 10⁻³) in HUFS African Americans.
source: Self-reported use of any lipid medication (coded as yes/no) was associated with increased risk of hypertension (p=1.25 × 10−3) but increasing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol remained associated with decreased risk of hypertension (p=4.46 × 10−2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis accounting for lipid medications.

claim: Increasing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol remained associated with decreased risk of hypertension (p=4.46 × 10⁻²) even after accounting for lipid medications in HUFS African Americans.
source: Self-reported use of any lipid medication (coded as yes/no) was associated with increased risk of hypertension (p=1.25 × 10−3) but increasing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol remained associated with decreased risk of hypertension (p=4.46 × 10−2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis accounting for lipid medications.

claim: For each of the selected covariates, the Akaike information criterion was larger for the model containing a term that interacted with age.
source: For each of the selected covariates, the Akaike information criterion was larger for the model containing a term that interacted with age (Table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by AIC values presented in Table 6.

claim: The evidence does not support time-dependence for any of the selected covariates.
source: Thus, the evidence does not support time-dependence for any of the selected covariates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the AIC analysis showing worse fit with interaction terms.

claim: Under the 2017 revised classification of hypertension (SBP ≥130 mm Hg or DBP ≥80 mm Hg), the prevalence of hypertension in HUFS increased from 48.3% to 66.1%.
source: Under these more stringent thresholds, the prevalence of hypertension increased from 48.3% to 66.1%, the median time to hypertension decreased to 36 years (95% CI [33, 39]), the age at maximum hazard increased to 57 (95% CI [33, 72]) years, and the lifetime risk at 85 years of age increased to 95.8% (95% CI [90.3%, 99.2%]).
evidence: This claim is supported by reanalysis of HUFS data using the 2017 revised thresholds.

claim: Under the 2017 revised classification, the median time to hypertension in HUFS decreased to 36 years (95% CI [33, 39]).
source: Under these more stringent thresholds, the prevalence of hypertension increased from 48.3% to 66.1%, the median time to hypertension decreased to 36 years (95% CI [33, 39]), the age at maximum hazard increased to 57 (95% CI [33, 72]) years, and the lifetime risk at 85 years of age increased to 95.8% (95% CI [90.3%, 99.2%]).
evidence: This claim is supported by reanalysis of HUFS data using the 2017 revised thresholds.

claim: Under the 2017 revised classification, the age at maximum hazard in HUFS increased to 57 (95% CI [33, 72]) years.
source: Under these more stringent thresholds, the prevalence of hypertension increased from 48.3% to 66.1%, the median time to hypertension decreased to 36 years (95% CI [33, 39]), the age at maximum hazard increased to 57 (95% CI [33, 72]) years, and the lifetime risk at 85 years of age increased to 95.8% (95% CI [90.3%, 99.2%]).
evidence: This claim is supported by reanalysis of HUFS data using the 2017 revised thresholds.

claim: Under the 2017 revised classification, the lifetime risk at 85 years of age in HUFS increased to 95.8% (95% CI [90.3%, 99.2%]).
source: Under these more stringent thresholds, the prevalence of hypertension increased from 48.3% to 66.1%, the median time to hypertension decreased to 36 years (95% CI [33, 39]), the age at maximum hazard increased to 57 (95% CI [33, 72]) years, and the lifetime risk at 85 years of age increased to 95.8% (95% CI [90.3%, 99.2%]).
evidence: This claim is supported by reanalysis of HUFS data using the 2017 revised thresholds.

claim: The inflection point in hazard rates is consistent with the log-normal parametric distribution yielding the best fit among the parametric distributions explored.
source: The Bayesian model of the hazard rates revealed an inflection point, consistent with the log-normal parametric distribution yielding the best fit among the parametric distributions we explored.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed inflection point to the best-fitting distribution.

claim: The simplest explanation for the inflection point in hazard rates is the change in trajectory of DBP, with the decrease in DBP leading to a decreased hazard of hypertension and consequently a reduced number of events.
source: We suggest that the simplest explanation for the inflection point in hazard rates is the change in trajectory of DBP, with the decrease in DBP leading to a decreased hazard of hypertension and consequently a reduced number of events.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors for the observed inflection point.

claim: The finding that the hazard rate does not reach zero (by 85 years of age) indicates the continued presence of risk.
source: We cannot rule out the possibility that there are individuals who are at less risk, although the finding that the hazard rate does not reach zero (by 85 years of age) indicates the continued presence of risk.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that hazard rates remain non-zero.

claim: It is possible that mortality due to comorbidities begins to subside by around 60 years of age, leading to reduced hazard rates of hypertension in older ages.
source: It is also possible that mortality due to comorbidities begins to subside by around 60 years of age, leading to reduced hazard rates of hypertension in older ages.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors for the observed decrease in hazard rates.

claim: Studies of hypertension using a case-control design should always include a logistic regression adjustment for both linear and quadratic effects of age.
source: Therefore, we recommend that studies of hypertension using a case-control design should always include a logistic regression adjustment for both linear and quadratic effects of age.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the finding that proportional hazards and logistic regression with age and age² provide comparable fits.

claim: The permanent stayer fraction essentially corresponded to the fraction of individuals who had not yet become hypertensive at the last observed age.
source: We found that the permanent stayer fraction essentially corresponded to the fraction of individuals who had not yet become hypertensive at the last observed age.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The assumption that the event will occur for every individual at some point in time, unless the individual dies first, is valid for hypertension.
source: A major implication for proportional hazards analysis is that the assumption that the event will occur for every individual at some point in time, unless the individual dies first, is valid.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that the permanent stayer fraction did not improve model fit.

claim: Controls in logistic regression should be interpreted as individuals that have not yet become hypertensive, rather than as individuals who will not become hypertensive.
source: A major implication for logistic regression is that controls should be interpreted as individuals that have not yet become hypertensive, rather than as individuals who will not become hypertensive.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that there are no true controls.

claim: Traditional risk factors for hypertension include excess body weight, excess dietary sodium intake, reduced physical activity, deficiency of potassium, and excess alcohol intake.
source: Traditional risk factors for hypertension include excess body weight, excess dietary sodium intake, reduced physical activity, deficiency of potassium, and excess alcohol intake (Chobanian et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chobanian et al., 2003.

claim: Excess weight and low potassium, but not excess sodium, were confirmed as risk factors in the multiple regression model.
source: One, we confirmed that excess weight and low potassium, but not excess sodium, were risk factors in our multiple regression model.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model selection results.

claim: Chloride was negatively associated with hypertension.
source: We found that chloride was negatively associated with hypertension.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression coefficients from the analysis.

claim: Lower serum chloride levels have been associated with higher risks of hypertension and cardiovascular disease and higher all-cause and cause-specific mortality among hypertensives.
source: Although high dietary intake of chloride is a risk factor for hypertension, lower serum chloride levels have been associated with higher risks of hypertension and cardiovascular disease and higher all-cause and cause-specific mortality among hypertensives (McCallum et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McCallum et al., 2013 and Taylor et al., 2007.

claim: In the Framingham Heart Study, the incidence rate of hypertension increased faster in females than in males, with females having lower incidence under 50 years of age and higher incidence over 50 years of age.
source: Two, longitudinal analysis of 30 years of follow-up in the Framingham Heart Study showed that the incidence rate of hypertension increased faster in females than in males, with females having lower incidence under 50 years of age and higher incidence over 50 years of age (Dannenberg et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dannenberg et al., 1988.

claim: Sex was not a significant covariate in the model selection.
source: In contrast, we found that sex was not a significant covariate, although low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, uric acid, and weight showed sex dimorphisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model selection results.

claim: The findings regarding hazard rates at early ages are consistent with low birth weight being a risk factor for hypertension.
source: Three, we did not have data on birth weight, but our findings regarding hazard rates at early ages are consistent with low birth weight being a risk factor for hypertension (Lackland et al., 2003) and African Americans having lower birth weight than European Americans (David and Collins, 1997).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed early hazard rates to known risk factors from the literature.

claim: African Americans have lower birth weight than European Americans.
source: Three, we did not have data on birth weight, but our findings regarding hazard rates at early ages are consistent with low birth weight being a risk factor for hypertension (Lackland et al., 2003) and African Americans having lower birth weight than European Americans (David and Collins, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to David and Collins, 1997.

claim: Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol has been reported to be positively associated with hypertension, but this association generally does not remain significant after covariate adjustment.
source: Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol has been reported to be positively associated with hypertension, but this association generally does not remain significant after covariate adjustment (Haffner et al., 1992; Laaksonen et al., 2008; Otsuka et al., 2016; Sesso et al., 2005; Wildman et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The opposite direction of effect of LDL cholesterol was not due to other (known) covariates.
source: We obtained a negative association in both single and multiple regression models, suggesting that the opposite direction of effect was not due to other (known) covariates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing single and multiple regression results.

claim: The opposite direction of effect of LDL cholesterol was not due to a time-dependent effect.
source: We also found that the opposite direction of effect was not due to a time-dependent effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the time-dependence analysis.

claim: The opposite direction of effect of LDL cholesterol was not due to confounding by self-reported use of medication (i.e. statins).
source: Furthermore, the opposite direction of effect was not due to confounding by self-reported use of medication (i.e. statins).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis accounting for lipid medications.

claim: Studies of the relationship between low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and healthy aging have led to conflicting conclusions.
source: Studies of the relationship between low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and healthy aging have led to conflicting conclusions, with some studies reporting a negative association (Barzilai et al., 2001; Postmus et al., 2015) and other studies reporting a positive association (Lv et al., 2015; Lv et al., 2019; Rantanen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies with conflicting results.

claim: One possible explanation for the discrepancy in LDL cholesterol associations is survival bias, if individuals with higher low-density lipoprotein cholesterol disproportionately experience mortality prior to the onset of hypertension.
source: One possible explanation for this discrepancy is survival bias, if individuals with higher low-density lipoprotein cholesterol disproportionately experience mortality prior to the onset of hypertension.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Uric acid is associated with hypertension, but whether this association is causal remains unestablished.
source: Uric acid is associated with hypertension, but whether this association is causal remains unestablished.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding uric acid and hypertension.

claim: Mendelian randomization studies have provided conflicting evidence regarding the causality of uric acid for hypertension.
source: Mendelian randomization (MR) studies have provided conflicting evidence regarding the causality of uric acid for hypertension, with evidence for no effect (Palmer et al., 2013), protection (Sedaghat et al., 2014), and risk (Parsa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple MR studies with conflicting results.

claim: MR studies have reported that uric acid is not causal for adiposity, chronic kidney disease, triglycerides, type 2 diabetes, or obesity.
source: MR studies have reported that uric acid is not causal for adiposity, chronic kidney disease, triglycerides, type 2 diabetes, or obesity (Jordan et al., 2019; Kleber et al., 2015; Lyngdoh et al., 2012; Rasheed et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple MR studies.

claim: Higher adiposity, higher body mass index, lower high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and higher triglycerides are causally associated with increased uric acid.
source: In contrast, higher adiposity, higher body mass index, lower high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and higher triglycerides are causally associated with increased uric acid (Lyngdoh et al., 2012; Palmer et al., 2013; Rasheed et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2019).
